title: Federated missing-nodes set is shared between concurrent requests
body:
Roadmap: spec/10 M24, T24.11.

`Federated::missing` is one shared mutex, so two `GET /lists` requests at the same time can overwrite each other's missing set. This predates the upstream sync. The two serial reads on a replica's `GET /lists` (`Read::Lists`, then `Read::ListHits`) could also become one round.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Merged into feat/ipam-integrations at 1f6266f.

title: Benchmark on quiet hardware: special names, upstream budget, device names
body:
Roadmap: spec/10 M24, T24.1 and T24.3 *Open* notes.

Docker Desktop can't give a 5% verdict: every UDP `bind()` there takes about 10 ms, and run-to-run noise was 20–35%. On the homelab (a Pi or a Linux host, the load generator on separate cores), with at least 5 alternating rounds:
- `make bench-smoke` for the special-names classifier (ADR-904) and upstream's last-healthy-member budget (UPS-006, ADR-165);
- names in DNS with `--devices 1000` against `--no-device-domain`, and check the roughly 4–5 KiB per device of RSS with `bench/memprobe.py`.

Harness bugs found on the way:
- `parse_dnsperf` fails with `no 'stddev' line` at very high qps (probably a non-numeric StdDev);
- the p99 overflow bucket (1.8e19 µs) leaks into `compare`.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller

title: Six tests fail on a Windows (CRLF) checkout

On a checkout with `core.autocrlf=true`, these tests fail because they compare files byte for byte or search for `\n`-joined text:

- `ops_004_signature_and_checksums`, `ops_004_update_check_and_swap`, `ops_004_refuses_bad_signature_or_checksum`, `ops_004_index_signature_is_checked`
- `clu_002_federated_covers_every_backend_read`
- `nfr_003_unsafe_is_forbidden_outside_telltale_net`

The API snapshot tests (`api_001_committed_openapi`, `agt_006_committed`) fail the same way until regenerated. A `.gitattributes` with `eol=lf` for fixtures, snapshots and Cargo.toml (or tests that normalise line endings) would fix it.

title: PBI: Live network map with animated query flows, colour-coded by health
body:
**PBI: Live network map with animated query flows (M26)**

**As** the owner of a home network, **I want** a live, animated map of my network and of where its lookups go, colour-coded by health, **so that** I can see at a glance what is talking, where it's going, and what is failing.

Roadmap: `spec/10` M26 (T26.1–T26.6). Requirements: OBS-901, OBS-902 (proposed).

## Two views

**1. Network map (the LAN):**
- **What it shows:** the gateway, then networks and VLANs, then devices, all from the M22 inventory, with switches and ports once M25's SNMP/LLDP data exists. The TelltaleDNS nodes and their upstreams are drawn too.
- **Flows:** animated pulses travel device → TelltaleDNS node → upstream (or local answer, cache, or block). Line width follows the query rate.
- **Interaction:** click a device to open its queries, Explain and anomalies. You can filter by VLAN, group or device.

**2. World view:**
- Animated arcs from your network to the countries and networks that answers point to, as a stream of recent lookups.
- It uses an **optional IP-to-country database downloaded at runtime**, never in the image (NFR-001: ≤ 15 MiB). Without it, the view says so and the network map still works.

## Colour code (both views)
| Colour | Meaning (examples) |
|---|---|
| 🟢 green | healthy: answered normally, upstream breaker closed |
| 🟡 yellow | warning: slow answer (over the latency SLO), upstream half-open or degraded, a device with an open anomaly finding, a high blocked share |
| 🔴 red | error: SERVFAIL, timeout, upstream down (breaker open), a node or replica not answering |

The thresholds come from the existing SLO and health settings, and are adjustable in the UI.

## Acceptance criteria
- **Data:** built on existing streams and counters (the query tail, time buckets, upstream health, cluster health). **Nothing is added to the DNS query path** (02 §3, CLU-004). The server samples and caps events per second for the map, and `bench-smoke` shows no regression.
- **Footprint:** no heavy graph or map library, only SVG or Canvas. The UI stays within its 400 KiB gzipped budget. Animation pauses when the tab is hidden, and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- **Cluster:** shows every node, using the federated reads like the other cluster views.
- **UI rule:** the whole feature is controlled from the UI: views, filters, thresholds, the GeoIP download (a toggle and its status), and the sampling rate. It is role-gated and has help topics.
- **Agent-ready:** the API serves the map data (a snapshot plus a stream), documented in OpenAPI; an MCP read tool gives the current health summary.
- **Tests:** Playwright for both views, the colour states, and reduced motion. Unit tests for the health classification.
- **Docs:** `docs/running.md` and a site page.

## Open questions (for the design ADR)
- Which GeoIP source and licence (a CC-BY "lite" country database, for example): its download URL, how often it updates, and verifying it.
- Whether the world view also places upstreams such as DoH providers, or only answer addresses.
author: nbacheller

title: chrono is unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2026-0543): ignored in deny.toml, replace when the OIDC library allows
body:
cargo-deny started failing on 2026-11-17 with RUSTSEC-2026-0543 (chrono unmaintained). It is an unmaintained notice, not a vulnerability.

chrono arrives through openidconnect 4.1 and oauth2 5.0 (OIDC sign-in, API-004); telltale-api also uses it directly for the clock feature.

For now deny.toml ignores the advisory with a reason. To close this:
- drop telltale-api's direct chrono use (std time or the time crate), and
- move to an openidconnect/oauth2 release without chrono, or reassess at each upstream sync.

Image delta of the ignore: none.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Scoped 2026-11-17 as T24.23 in spec/10. Decision: Replace the OIDC library (openidconnect/oauth2 pull chrono) with one without it or a minimal code+PKCE flow on existing crates; design ADR first, then drop the deny.toml ignore.

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Merged into feat/ipam-integrations (wave m).

title: e2e: hard-coded metrics, stub-upstream and ntfy ports stop two Playwright runs sharing a host
body:
Found in the review of the #63/#64 auth fix (2026-11-17). Deferred because CI runs one suite at a time.

Only the HTTP, DNS and mDNS ports read env vars (`ui/tests/e2e/ports.ts`). These are still fixed:
- metrics 19154: `ui/tests/e2e/server.mjs`, `1-ui.spec.ts`
- stub upstream 15399: `server.mjs`, `1-ui.spec.ts`
- ntfy fake 18997: `server.mjs`, `1-ui.spec.ts`

With 19154 held, the node exits with "Address already in use" before the API starts, so parallel local tracks collide.

Fix: derive these ports from `E2E_HTTP_PORT` (as an offset) or from env vars in `ports.ts`, and use them everywhere.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Scoped 2026-11-17 as T24.19 in spec/10. Decision: Derive every e2e port from E2E_HTTP_PORT as fixed offsets in ports.ts.

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Done in T24.19: ui/tests/e2e/ports.ts derives every port from E2E_HTTP_PORT (offsets 0 to 12). Open: the Keycloak realm for the OIDC spec still names 18054.

title: ups_005 parallel-race test fails when the upstream suite runs in parallel in the dev container
body:
`ups_005_parallel_races_and_first_answer_wins` (`crates/telltale-upstream/tests/upstream.rs:291`) fails every time in the wrendns-dev container when the `upstream` test binary runs in parallel (`cargo test -p telltale-upstream --test upstream`), with "did not wait for the slow member": the parallel group took 150 ms or more although the fast member answers in 5 ms. It passes alone, passes with `--test-threads=1`, and passes in fork CI. It fails the same way at 1f6266f, so it predates wave m.

The suite takes about 67 s in parallel (132 s serially), so some sibling test holds something for a long time; the race may be with that test's fake servers or a shared resource, not CPU load (the container's load average was 0.08).

To do: find what the sibling tests share with this one, and fix the cause rather than raising the 150 ms bound.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Fixed: the test measured the kernel-wide UDP bind queue in Docker Desktop, not the race. It is now judged by outcome and by the gap after the fast member's reply (ADR-974). 20 of 20 parallel runs pass in wrendns-dev. Removing the per-query bind from the product is T24.25, behind a benchmark.

title: CMDB: configuration items from many sources, a definitive source per attribute, and MACD lifecycle
body:
## What

A CMDB: one configuration item (CI) per real thing on the network, built from every source that reports on it, with each source's record kept and linked, a declared definitive source per piece of information, and a managed lifecycle (MACD: move, add, change, delete).

## Why

Several sources already report on the same devices, and more are coming:
- the UniFi gateway and Home Assistant (M22);
- SNMP on the gateway and switches (M25);
- imported nmap/CSV scans (T25.11);
- Pi-hole imports, DHCP leases, the query log's client attribution, and Kubernetes workloads.

They disagree: names, addresses, vendors, locations. The M25 inventory merges records by MAC, but it doesn't say which source wins for which field, keep each source's view next to the merged one, or track a device's changes over time. A CMDB pulls all the signals in, builds the CI with its linked sources, and lets the owner say which source is definitive for which information. Ingesting from many sources then gives one answer that they all agree on.

## Scope (to be fixed by the design ADR)

- **CIs and types:** devices, interfaces, networks/VLANs, TelltaleDNS nodes, services and upstreams, and their relations (on network, attached to switch port, member of group).
- **Linked source records:** every source's record is kept as reported, with when it was last seen, and linked to its CI. Nothing is lost when sources disagree.
- **Reconciliation:** identity matching across sources (MAC first, then serial, a router's client ID, a hostname plus a network), with manual link and unlink.
- **Definitive source:** a precedence per attribute (for example: name from Home Assistant, location from UniFi, vendor from SNMP, owner set by hand), an override per CI, and a conflict view of where sources disagree with the definitive value.
- **MACD lifecycle:** move, add, change and delete as recorded changes on a CI (requested, approved, done), with history and audit. Optionally, detected changes such as a new device, a moved port or a disappeared device raise a MACD to confirm.
- **API, MCP and UI:** read and query CIs and their sources, set precedence, handle MACDs. The UI has a CI page with its sources side by side, and the standing UI rule applies.
- **Rules carried over from M25:** read-only towards devices, off the DNS path, bounded storage, privacy levels respected, the cluster's single management plane.

Roadmap: M31 in spec/10 (T31.1 is the design).
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Owner request 2026-11-18: click a device and see its applied filters and policies. Built first as T24.30, a device's effective policy: the group and the key that matched it, lists and categories, SafeSearch, schedules and whether they're in effect, rules, and the upstream group. It's a Policy panel on the Clients page now, and the CMDB CI page (T31.5) reuses it.

title: Sandboxed workers fail in release builds: RLIMIT_DATA vs mimalloc (Pi-hole import broken); no /tmp in the image
body:
In every musl release build (amd64 and arm64), the Pi-hole import fails with `this isn't a Pi-hole export the import can read: <path>: <path>`, even for a valid v6 Teleporter zip or gravity.db. The debug glibc builds used by the tests work.

**Cause (strace):** `telltale_net::worker::harden` sets `RLIMIT_DATA` to 1 GiB. The next `mprotect(..., PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE)` fails with `ENOMEM`: mimalloc, the release build's allocator, has reserved address space that counts against the limit. SQLite's open then returns no handle, and rusqlite reports that as the bare path. The discovery workers use the same hardening.

**Second issue:** the scratch image has no `/tmp`, and the Teleporter path writes its temporary gravity.db with `std::env::temp_dir()`.

Found while importing a Pi-hole Teleporter export on the Pi-hole pair. Fix track: `feat/worker-rlimit-mimalloc`. It adds a release-build CI check, so the tests stop missing this.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body: Fixed: workers set MIMALLOC_ARENA_RESERVE=0, so RLIMIT_DATA bounds what they really hold (ADR-988), and the import unpacks into a private directory under the data directory (ADR-989). Release-build checks added to CI.

title: Content categories like UniFi: grouped category checkboxes per client group, backed by maintained open lists
body:
Owner request 2026-11-18: organize blocking into content categories like UniFi's content filtering. Categories sit in groups such as Adult and Sensitive Content, AI & Crypto, New or Risky Domains, and Security & Threat Protection. Each group has checkboxes per category, an "n of m" count and info icons, and the selection is made per client group.

Only categories backed by a maintained open list are offered. UniFi's commercial classification covers 100+ categories, but open lists don't exist for many of them (Religion, Sports, Travel and so on). Lists are downloaded at runtime and never bundled, and each source's licence is recorded.

This changes the upstream scope note "not parental controls: no content categories" (ADR-994). The design is T24.29 (ADR-994, ADR-995), on branch feat/t24.29-content-categories-design; owner decisions come after the design.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body:
Added 2026-11-18: filter profiles like UniFi's content-filter editor.
- **Profile list:** name, source, filter scope, SafeSearch and schedule.
- **Editor:** a source picker for networks/VLANs and individual devices, warning when a device uses a private MAC; an ad-block switch; SafeSearch per engine (Google, Bing, YouTube); a filtering level of Off, Enhanced (the category picker) or Basic (adult and malicious only); and a category picker with search and select all/none.
- **Model:** a profile maps onto the existing group, which already has sources, SafeSearch, blocked services and weekly schedules. The design covers the gaps. Same design track (T24.29).

title: Two-way UniFi sync of devices and groups
body:
Owner request 2026-11-18: sync devices and groups between TelltaleDNS and UniFi in both directions. A device added to a group in UniFi joins the linked group in TelltaleDNS, and the reverse.

UniFi's content filtering works on traffic and applies regardless of DNS. TelltaleDNS filters DNS and adds per-device visibility, and the sync keeps the two consistent.

Writes to the gateway need an ADR and owner approval: ADR-998 covers the sync, ADR-999 covers UniFi write access. The design is T25.18, on branch feat/t25.18-unifi-sync-design. It covers explicit links per group, a definitive side or two-way with a conflict view, a dry-run preview before the first sync, least-privilege write-only credentials and plan-only agents, and it ties into the CMDB's definitive-source model (#21). Tests run against a fake UniFi API only.
author: nbacheller

comments.author: nbacheller
comments.body:
Design merged (ADR-998 and ADR-999), and all of the owner's recommendations are accepted. The read direction ships first. The build follows T25.10.

Measured from a VLAN on a test network: UniFi content filtering is DNS-level. The gateway sinkholes filtered names (to an address of its own) and intercepts outbound port-53 queries. Queries to an internal resolver (such as an existing resolver's VIP) are not intercepted, and HTTPS to a real address isn't blocked. So devices that use TelltaleDNS are filtered by TelltaleDNS's categories (T24.29), or by the gateway when TelltaleDNS forwards to it from the device's VLAN (T24.31 and T24.32). The owner chose both.

title: Map: giant legend icons; nodes shown Failing for a dead spare upstream; no hint for IPv6 upstreams without an IPv6 route
body:
Seen on a three-node Raspberry Pi cluster (http://<node>:8053/#/map).

1. **Giant legend symbols.** The legend's Failing and Warning icons render at hundreds of pixels, filling the page below the map. They're SVGs with no size constraint in the legend.
2. **Nodes marked Failing because of a dead spare upstream.** node-a, node-b and node-c all show red "Failing" although every query is answered. The cause is two IPv6 upstreams (pihole-1 and pihole-2, Cloudflare's [2606:4700:4700::1111] and [::1001], imported from Pi-hole). They fail because the hosts have no IPv6 default route. ADR-970 §5 colours a resolver by the worst of what is downstream of it, so one dead member of a `fastest` group with healthy siblings turns the node red. That's misleading: a group that still answers should be yellow at most, naming the dead member.
3. **No hint about the cause.** Neither the importer nor the upstream health says "this host has no IPv6 route". The Upstreams page and the importer preview should flag an IPv6 upstream on a node without IPv6 connectivity (and the same for IPv4).
author: nbacheller

title: Upstreams: a simple provider picker like Pi-hole's, with the technical view as Advanced; wrong "config file" label
body:
Owner request 2026-11-18: make upstreams easy for a general user, the way Pi-hole does it.

- **Simple view (the default):** checkboxes for well-known public providers (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, OpenDNS, AdGuard, Mullvad, CleanBrowsing and others from presets/upstreams.toml). Each has its filtering variant where one exists, such as Cloudflare for Families or Quad9 unfiltered vs. filtered. There's one choice of transport (encrypted DoT/DoH, recommended, or plain), IPv4 and/or IPv6 entries (IPv6 greyed out with a reason when the node has no IPv6 route), and a "custom" row to type an address or URL.
- **Advanced view:** today's technical list and form, kept.
- **Bug:** every upstream shows "config file", including the four imported from Pi-hole through the API (stored as managed entries). The source label is wrong.

title: PBI: cloud-hosted resolver (free Azure tier) with DoH setup for Windows, macOS, Android and iOS
body:
**Owner request (2026-11-18):** a cloud-hosted TelltaleDNS that phones and laptops use when they're away from home. It needs a DoH client setup for Windows, macOS, Android and iOS. Hosting on a free Azure tier is preferred.

Roadmap: **M32** in `spec/10-roadmap-and-tasks.md` (T32.1–T32.9).

## What exists already
- **Encrypted listeners:** DoT, DoH (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) and DoQ are built (T4.5, T7.7, T7.8; ADR-039).
- **Per-device identity:** a device is identified by its DoH path (`/dns-query/<id>`) or by a DoT/DoQ SNI label under a wildcard certificate, and that works on mobile data (FLT-006, ADR-976).
- **DDR** is built (ADR-904).
- **Limits:** per-address connection caps and rate limits exist.
- **Certificates** are read from files and reloaded when they change.

## Gaps found
1. **Access is IP-only.** `[access] allowed_networks` is checked before the client ID (`pipeline.rs`). Letting roaming devices in means `0.0.0.0/0`, which makes the resolver open to anyone over DoH and DoT. There's no "a known client ID is required" gate.
2. **No built-in ACME.** Certificates come only from files. A per-device SNI ID needs a wildcard certificate, which means DNS-01.
3. **No device setup profiles:** no `.mobileconfig`, no Windows script, no Android page.
4. **No cloud deployment material**, for Azure or anywhere else.
5. **SQLite WAL isn't safe on SMB** (Azure Files). A cloud node needs ephemeral storage, with its config from Git or from the home cluster.
6. **A promised check is missing:** spec/08 says startup warns when a listener is bound to a public IP, but it isn't implemented.

## Azure hosting (Microsoft's pages, checked 2026-11-18)
| Option | DoH 443 | DoT 853 (Android) | UDP 53 | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Container Apps, Consumption, scale to zero | yes, free managed cert | no | no | free within the grant (180k vCPU-s, 360k GiB-s, 2M requests a month), but a 10–30 s cold start |
| Container Apps, 1 replica always on (0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GiB) | yes | no | no | about **$4–14/month** above the grant |
| Container Apps on your own VNet (TCP ingress) | yes | yes | no | adds about $25/month (load balancer and public IPs) |
| Free-account VM (B1s / B2pts v2 / B2ats v2, 750 h/month) | yes | yes | yes | free for **12 months only**; a static public IP is about $3.65/month |
| App Service F1 Free | no | no | no | unworkable: 60 CPU-min/day, no custom-domain TLS |

**Summary:** no Azure option is free forever *and* serves Android natively. Container Apps covers Windows and Apple over DoH, cheaply. The 12-month VM covers everything for a year.

## Clients
- **Windows 11:** native DoH. Register the server with `Add-DnsClientDohServerAddress` or `netsh dnsclient add encryption`, using a template URL that carries the device's path token. Group Policy and Intune can require it. Windows 10 has no native DoH client and would need dnscrypt-proxy (ISC licence).
- **macOS 11+ and iOS/iPadOS 14+:** native, through a `.mobileconfig` DNS Settings payload (DoH ServerURL with the path token, or DoT ServerName), with OnDemand rules. mTLS works on iOS 16+ and macOS 13+. In OS 27 the payload is deprecated in favour of the declarative `com.apple.configuration.network.dns-settings`, so ship both.
- **Android:** the built-in Private DNS is **DoT only**, by hostname, e.g. `<device>.dns.example`. DoH needs an app, e.g. Rethink DNS (Apache-2.0), or Chrome's per-app Secure DNS template.

## Proposed tasks (M32)
- T32.1 public-listener gate
- T32.2 cloud profile (stateless)
- T32.3 Azure Container Apps template
- T32.4 Azure VM template
- T32.5 certificates (ACME)
- T32.6 device onboarding page and profiles
- T32.7 client apps decision
- T32.8 one policy at home and away
- T32.9 closing

The details are in spec/10.

## Owner decisions (to ask together when M32 starts)
1. **Hosting:** Container Apps (DoH only, about $4–14/month always on, or free with cold starts), the 12-month free VM (every protocol), or both templates.
2. **Android:** DoT (needs the VM, or Container Apps on a VNet) or an app.
3. **Client apps:** build our own, or document permissive third-party clients (Rethink DNS, dnscrypt-proxy).
4. **Domain and certificates:** which domain, and which DNS provider for DNS-01 wildcard certificates.
5. **Home and away:** the cloud node joins the home cluster, or shares its config through Git.
6. **Query log in the cloud:** retention, and where it's kept.
author: nbacheller

title: Enhancement: temporary site exceptions from a browser add-on or a landing page
body:
**Owner request (2026-11-18):** a browser add-on or a landing page that lets someone make a temporary exception for a site that's blocked.

Roadmap: **T24.39** in `spec/10-roadmap-and-tasks.md`.

## What exists already
- **Quick rules** (ADR-067): allow a domain for a set time, for one device, one group or everyone. They expire on their own and are audited. The API is `PUT /api/v1/rules/{id}`, with the agent scope `config:write:rules`.
- **"Make a quick rule"** sits in the query log's "Why?" drawer, but only for someone signed in to the admin UI.

## The catch with a landing page
A blocked name could resolve to TelltaleDNS, which would then serve a "this site is blocked" page. That works for plain HTTP only. For HTTPS, which is nearly every site, the browser shows a certificate error before any page appears, and sites on the HSTS preload list can't be clicked through at all. So:
- **The browser add-on is the reliable route.** A Chrome/Edge/Firefox (MV3) extension sees a lookup fail or come back with the block answer, explains why the site is blocked, and offers "Allow for 15 min / 1 h / today", or "Ask for access".
- **The landing page** is a TelltaleDNS page the user opens themselves, e.g. `http://telltale.lan/unblock`. They type or paste the site, see why it's blocked, and request or grant an exception. It can also be the HTTP block page for plain-HTTP sites.

## Proposed scope
1. **Exception requests:** a new request object (site, device, reason, duration asked for), stored, audited and replicated.
   - **Policy per group:** either self-serve up to a limit (say 15 min, N a day), or "ask a parent/admin". Some categories are never allowed (threat, adult); those come from T24.29's categories.
   - **Approval:** a notification (UI badge plus the existing alert sinks), and one-click approve or deny that creates a quick rule scoped to that device.
2. **Device-scoped tokens:** the add-on and the page identify the device without admin rights.
   - A token can only create or ask for its own device's exceptions, inside its group's limits. It's rate limited.
   - It pairs by QR code or a code from the device page. It is never an admin token.
3. **Landing page:** `/unblock`, phone-width and reachable from the LAN. It shows the explanation (the same text as Explain, "blocked by list X / category Y") and the request or self-serve controls.
4. **Browser extension:** the MV3 extension, permissive licence, in this repo. Store listings are optional.
   - **Detecting a block:** the extension can't read DNS answers directly. It uses the navigation error plus a query to the TelltaleDNS API: "is `<host>` blocked for me, and why?"
   - **Limiting the data:** it sends only the host name, nothing about the page or history.
5. **Shared work:** API, MCP (requests readable by agents; approval plan-only), help topics, Playwright for the page, extension tests (Puppeteer or Playwright with the extension loaded), and the cluster e2e (a request made on a replica appears on the primary).

## Owner decisions (to ask when it starts)
1. Self-serve or approval, per group (default: approval for kids' groups, self-serve with a limit for adults).
2. Durations offered and daily caps.
3. Categories that can never be excepted.
4. Browsers: Chrome/Edge (MV3) first, Firefox next, Safari later or never.
5. Store listings, or load the extension unpacked/self-hosted only.
6. Whether a plain-HTTP block page is served at all (it means answering blocked names with this node's IP instead of NXDOMAIN/0.0.0.0).
author: nbacheller
